arrive.title: Where do useful features come from?
arrive.body1: Lesson 6 left you with a question. A model can be given examples and a task without being told which features to look for – so where do those useful features come from?
arrive.body2: To answer it, we'll work with something you already have opinions about: music. No production tools, no theory. Just a booth to listen in, and a board where tracks that belong together can sit side by side.

predictPick.title: Which of these belongs in a workout playlist?
predictPick.subhead: Listen to a few seconds of each song, then choose the ones you'd want to hear during a workout. There's no right answer yet – we'll use your choices to explore what makes one song feel like a good fit.

predictName.title: What made you pick them?
predictName.subhead: What did you notice about the songs you chose?
predictName.hold: Hold onto that list. Next you'll try to turn it into a system that picks workout songs for you.
predictName.cta: Turn your list into a detector

handRules.title: Turn your list into a rule for 'workout song'
handRules.body: Here are the measurements you picked, as sliders. Set a threshold for each – how fast, how loud, how much bass a song needs before your detector calls it a workout song.

handTest.subhead: A fresh batch plays. You judge first – belongs or doesn't – while the detector's guess stays hidden. Then we reveal what your detector said and the true answer. The score is how often the detector was actually right.
handTest.promptLine: Judge each song – belongs or doesn't. The detector stays hidden until you do.
handTest.adjustReadout: With these thresholds: {hits} of {n} correct against the true labels.

handWall.title: You can keep changing the thresholds, but you run into a problem.
handWall.contrastA: A song can have a fast tempo and a strong beat and still not belong in the playlist.
handWall.contrastB: Another song can break the rules you chose and still feel like a good match.
handWall.body2: The measurements give you useful information, but they don't tell you which combinations will matter.
handWall.body3: For a long time, one way of dealing with this was to have people choose the features for the system. But with something as complicated as music, there can be far too many possibilities to work out by hand.
handWall.pivot: What if we gave the system examples and let it learn which patterns are useful?

twoPaths.title: You just tried the first path. Here's the second.
twoPaths.path1: Hand-designed: You choose what to measure → you set the rules → result. (This was Step 3, and for years it was the only path.)
twoPaths.path2: Learned: You give examples → training → a learned arrangement → result.
twoPaths.body: On the second path you don't pick the measurements at all. You give examples of what belongs and what doesn't, and let training work out what's worth noting.

labelTrain.title: Mark a few. Then press train.
labelTrain.status: Rearranging by what the examples have in common…
labelTrain.drawingCaption: This board is our way of drawing what the model learned. The model isn't building a map inside – we are, so you can see it.

repReveal.title: You never told the model which features to use. You just gave it examples.
repReveal.tieBack: The model changed its weights as it trained, just as you saw earlier. But now those changes are doing something different: they're helping the model find a useful way of representing the songs.
repReveal.term: We call this a learned representation.
repReveal.body2: It doesn't have to be something simple like "fast" or "loud." The representation can involve a large number of numbers, and we may not be able to give each one a name.
repReveal.body3: What matters is that the representation contains information that helps with the task.
repReveal.cta: So how good is it, really?

headToHead.title: Your rules vs. what it learned
headToHead.body: Here's a fresh set of songs neither system has seen. Your hand-tuned detector scores them. So does the model that learned from your examples. Same songs, same answers to beat.
headToHead.predict: Before you run them – out of {n}, how many do you think each will get right?
headToHead.after1: A hand-picked list of measurements can only take you so far. There are too many possible patterns to decide in advance which ones will matter.
headToHead.after2: The model can learn those patterns from the examples instead.
headToHead.callback: Remember 'something I can't quite name'? That's the part your thresholds couldn't reach – and the part the learned representation could.
headToHead.cta: So what did it catch that you couldn't?

hidden.title: Are these two similar?
hidden.body1: Things like tempo, volume, and rhythm tell us something about a song, but not everything. Two songs can be similar on those measurements and still sound very different. Two others can be quite different and still sound like they belong together.
hidden.body2: A useful representation can capture relationships that aren't obvious from any single measurement. That's the part a hand-written list of features can't reach – and the part you felt was missing back when you picked 'something I can't quite name.'

taskDep.bridge: That arrangement was built to find workout songs. Keep the exact same songs – but change the job, and watch what starts to matter.
taskDep.title: Useful for what?
taskDep.helper: Open at least two. Notice what information becomes important in each.
taskDep.revealTitle: The same songs. A different 'useful' each time.
taskDep.revealBody1: There isn't one correct representation of these songs. What's worth keeping depends on the task you're training for.
taskDep.revealBody2: A representation that's great for 'make me sweat' can be nearly useless for 'sort by instrument' – the information each job leans on is different.
taskDep.clarification: The model isn't handed a list of what to keep. During training, the task – what counts as a right answer – is what pushes some information to matter and some to fall away.
taskDep.foundationNod: You might be wondering: then how does one AI seem to do everything? Some representations turn out useful for many tasks at once – that's a later story. For now, the point holds: useful depends on the job.
taskDep.cta: So does the model decide everything?

whoDecides.title: So does the model decide everything? No.
whoDecides.body: It found a useful arrangement without you naming the features. But it didn't run the whole show. People still made every big call around it:
whoDecides.keyLine: What changed isn't that people stopped deciding. It's that we no longer have to specify every useful feature by hand.
cards: The data – which songs it learned from.
The task – what job it was training for.
The training objective – what counts as a right answer.
The design – how the model is built and trained.
The check – whether the result is actually any good.

challenge.prompt: From these examples, can you describe exactly what makes a song belong?
challenge.after: You probably spotted some patterns. But could you write down every useful one – as a fixed list, in advance?
challenge.land: That's the gap learned representations fill. Instead of making you name every useful pattern up front, training adjusts the model – its weights, as you saw – until its representation is useful for the task.
challenge.cantPin: I couldn't pin it all down

reflection.title: Where do useful features come from?
reflection.beforeLabel: Before this lesson, I thought the useful features came from…
reflection.beforePlaceholder: someone measuring the right things… a list you write down…
reflection.afterPlaceholder: the model can learn them from examples and a task – and 'useful' depends on the job…

closing.before: A person chooses the features – tempo, bass, volume, vocals…
closing.after: The model learns a representation – patterns drawn from examples, for a task.
closing.body: For years, people designed or picked the features before training. Deep learning made it possible for models to learn useful representations straight from the data. That doesn't mean the model hears music the way you do – it means training can produce internal patterns useful for the job it was trained on.
closing.bankThen: The word itself isn't enough. What surrounds it matters.
closing.connective: You just saw that a useful representation depends on the task. For a word, the job is set by its neighbours – a useful representation of it can't be fixed in advance either. That's the next lesson.
closing.headline: What matters can depend on the company it keeps.

seoSpine.h1: What Are Learned Representations in AI?
seoSpine.lead: A representation is how a system encodes information so later steps can use it. Representation learning means useful encodings are discovered from data — not only chosen by hand.

sections.heading: Feature engineering vs representation learning
sections.body: Feature engineering is when people decide which measurements matter. Representation learning is when the model adjusts its own encoding during training, capturing patterns that are hard to specify in advance.

sections.heading: How neural networks learn features
sections.body: As weights change, the network’s internal features shift toward what helps the task. What information matters can change when the goal changes — the same raw input, different useful encodings.
